claim: Experience-dependent plasticity is a key feature of brain synapses for which neuronal N-Methyl-D-Aspartate receptors (NMDARs) play a major role, from developmental circuit refinement to learning and memory.
source: Experience-dependent plasticity is a key feature of brain synapses for which neuronal N-Methyl-D-Aspartate receptors (NMDARs) play a major role, from developmental circuit refinement to learning and memory.
evidence: This statement is supported by established scientific consensus about the role of neuronal NMDARs in plasticity and learning.

claim: Astrocytes express NMDARs, although their exact function has remained controversial.
source: Astrocytes also express NMDARs, although their exact function has remained controversial.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field, acknowledging controversy.

claim: GluN2C NMDAR is a subtype highly expressed in astrocytes in mouse hippocampus.
source: Here, we identify in mouse hippocampus, a circuit function for GluN2C NMDAR, a subtype highly expressed in astrocytes, in layer-specific tuning of synaptic strengths in CA1 pyramidal neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RT-PCR, immunoprecipitation, and reporter mouse experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: Interfering with astrocyte NMDAR or GluN2C NMDAR activity reduces the range of presynaptic strength distribution specifically in the stratum radiatum inputs without an appreciable change in the mean presynaptic strength.
source: Interfering with astrocyte NMDAR or GluN2C NMDAR activity reduces the range of presynaptic strength distribution specifically in the stratum radiatum inputs without an appreciable change in the mean presynaptic strength.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from pharmacological and genetic manipulations shown in Figures 1, 2, 6, and 7.

claim: Mathematical modeling shows that narrowing of the width of presynaptic release probability distribution compromises the expression of long-term synaptic plasticity.
source: Mathematical modeling shows that narrowing of the width of presynaptic release probability distribution compromises the expression of long-term synaptic plasticity.
evidence: This is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Astrocyte GluN2C NMDARs adjust basal synaptic weight distribution of Schaffer collateral inputs, which in turn impacts computations performed by the CA1 pyramidal neuron.
source: Our findings suggest a novel feedback signaling system that uses astrocyte GluN2C NMDARs to adjust basal synaptic weight distribution of Schaffer collateral inputs, which in turn impacts computations performed by the CA1 pyramidal neuron.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental and modeling data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The distribution of synaptic strengths is thought to reflect the capacity or the state of information storage of neural circuits.
source: In particular, the distribution of synaptic strengths is thought to reflect the capacity or the state of information storage of neural circuits (Barbour et al., 2007; Buzsáki and Mizuseki, 2014; Bromer et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: NMDARs are heteromeric assemblies consisting of four subunits, and seven NMDAR subunit genes have been identified that fall into three subfamilies: Grin1 encoding the obligatory GluN1 subunit, four Grin2 genes encoding GluN2A-D, and two Grin3 genes encoding GluN3A-B.
source: NMDARs are heteromeric assemblies consisting of four subunits, and seven NMDAR subunit genes have been identified that fall into three subfamilies: Grin1 encoding the obligatory GluN1 subunit, four Grin2 genes encoding GluN2A-D, and two Grin3 genes encoding GluN3A-B (Paoletti et al., 2013; Hansen et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge about NMDAR structure supported by citations.

claim: NMDARs are involved in pathological conditions such as epilepsy, ischemia, and traumatic brain injury.
source: NMDARs are also involved in pathological conditions such as epilepsy, ischemia, and traumatic brain injury (Hansen et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: NMDARs in oligodendrocytes play a role in axonal energy metabolism.
source: Amongst the better characterized glial NMDARs, NMDARs in oligodendrocytes play a role in axonal energy metabolism (Saab et al., 2016) and exacerbate pathological conditions (Káradóttir et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: There are reports of GluN2C mRNA expression in astrocytes in the adult brain.
source: Nevertheless, there are reports of GluN2C mRNA expression in astrocytes in the adult brain (Watanabe et al., 1993; Karavanova et al., 2007; Ravikrishnan et al., 2018), and several studies provide physiological evidence in support of astrocyte NMDAR expression under non-pathological conditions (Schipke et al., 2001; Serrano et al., 2008; Lalo et al., 2006; Letellier et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Astrocytes regulate a diverse set of essential brain activities, from neurovascular coupling, metabolic support, and ionic homeostasis to synaptic connectivity and function.
source: Astrocytes regulate a diverse set of essential brain activities, from neurovascular coupling, metabolic support, and ionic homeostasis (e.g. Attwell et al., 2010; Giaume et al., 2010; Simard and Nedergaard, 2004) to synaptic connectivity and function (e.g. Araque et al., 2014; Clarke and Barres, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Recent studies have highlighted a role for astrocytes in the bidirectional control of basal synaptic transmission.
source: Recent studies have highlighted a role for astrocytes in the bidirectional control of basal synaptic transmission (Panatier et al., 2011; Perea and Araque, 2007; Di Castro et al., 2011; Martin-Fernandez et al., 2017; Schwarz et al., 2017), which likely involves signaling via their perisynaptic processes (Bindocci et al., 2017; Bazargani and Attwell, 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: A single astrocyte, which contacts tens of thousands of synapses, can concurrently mediate bi-directional synapse regulation at separate synaptic contact sites.
source: Moreover, mounting evidence suggests that astrocytes are not only capable of either simply potentiating (Panatier et al., 2011; Perea and Araque, 2007; Jourdain et al., 2007) or depressing synaptic transmission (Martín et al., 2015; Pascual et al., 2005), but a single astrocyte, which contacts tens of thousands of synapses, can concurrently mediate bi-directional synapse regulation at separate synaptic contact sites (Schwarz et al., 2017; Covelo and Araque, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: MK801 (1 mM) infused into the postsynaptic cell via the patch pipette resulted in over 92% inhibition of synaptic NMDAR currents.
source: MK801 (1 mM) was infused into the postsynaptic cell via the patch pipette, and after 10–15 min but prior to starting the experiment, Schaffer collaterals were stimulated at 0.1 Hz for at least 45 times to pre-block synaptic NMDARs. This resulted in over 92 % inhibition of synaptic NMDAR currents (Bender et al., 2006; Figure 1—figure supplement 1; see Materials and Methods).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and cited methodology.

claim: The overall decrease in PPR variance by NMDAR antagonists was associated with a change in PPR (ΔPPR) that was negatively correlated to the baseline PPR.
source: This overall decrease in PPR variance, when examined at the level of individual inputs, was associated with a change in PPR (ΔPPR) that was negatively correlated to the baseline PPR: PPR of some inputs increased while others decreased by the NMDAR antagonist application (Figure 1E–G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E-G.

claim: A linear fit to the ΔPPR vs baseline PPR data intercepted the x-axis near the baseline mean PPR for MK801 (x-axis intercept: 1.97) and AP5 (x-axis intercept: 1.95).
source: Furthermore, consistent with a lack of change in the mean PPR upon blocking NMDARs, a linear fit to the data intercepted the x-axis near the baseline mean PPR (x-axis intercept: MK801 = 1.97; AP5 = 1.95).
evidence: This is an analysis of the data shown in Figure 1E-G.

claim: Bath applied MK801 did not substantially alter the amplitude of the first EPSC to the pair of stimuli relative to control slices.
source: On average, bath applied MK801 did not substantially alter the amplitude of the first EPSC to the pair of stimuli relative to control slices, despite a small tendency for an increase with a time delay (Figure 1I; p = 0.657).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I with statistical analysis.

claim: MK801 had little effect on CV–2 of EPSC amplitudes.
source: MK801 also had little effect on CV–2 of EPSC amplitudes (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B; p = 0.991), although the responses of individual inputs to MK801, albeit small in magnitude, were positively correlated to CV–2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D; Pearson's r = 0.420, p = 0.026) and negatively correlated to PPR (Figure 1—figure supplement 3H; Pearson's r = –0.474, p = 0.011).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B, D, H with statistical analysis.

claim: AP5 significantly increased EPSC amplitudes within 10 min of application.
source: In contrast to MK801, AP5 significantly increased EPSC amplitudes within 10 min of application (Figure 1J; p = 0.026), and the increase in CV–2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B; AP5 p = 0.003) suggested that the change in EPSC amplitude involved a presynaptic change.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1J and Figure 1—figure supplement 3B with statistical analysis.

claim: Ro25-6981 (10 µM), a GluN2B-specific NMDAR antagonist, had little effect on PPR variance.
source: We also tested for the contribution of GluN2B NMDAR and also of mGluR5 in maintaining PPR variance. Bath applying Ro25-6981 (10 µM), a GluN2B-specific NMDAR antagonist (Fischer et al., 1997), and MPEP (25 µM), an mGluR5-specific antagonist (Gasparini et al., 1999), had little effect on PPR variance (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A-C; Ro256981 p = 0.362, MPEP p = 0.349).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A-C with statistical analysis and citations for drug specificity.

claim: MPEP (25 µM), an mGluR5-specific antagonist, had little effect on PPR variance but significantly increased the mean PPR.
source: Bath applying Ro25-6981 (10 µM), a GluN2B-specific NMDAR antagonist (Fischer et al., 1997), and MPEP (25 µM), an mGluR5-specific antagonist (Gasparini et al., 1999), had little effect on PPR variance (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A-C; Ro256981 p = 0.362, MPEP p = 0.349). MPEP, however, significantly increased the mean PPR (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C; p = 0.033), which is consistent with a reported role for mGluR5 in presynaptic strength regulation (Panatier et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C with statistical analysis and citation to prior literature.

claim: Bath application of MK801 and AP5 reduced PPR disparity in two independent pathway analysis.
source: In this method, the absolute difference of PPRs between the two inputs (PPR disparity) is taken as a proxy for presynaptic strength variability, with lower PPR disparity indicating lower PPR variability and vice versa (Figure 1—figure supplement 5A,B). Note that graphs of the PPR difference contain a regression-to-the-mean component, which is however effectively cancelled out when making direct graph comparisons, within the same parametric space. Consistent with our analysis thus far, bath application of MK801 and AP5 reduced PPR disparity (Figure 1—figure supplement 5D,E; MK801 p = 0.001, AP5 p = 0.004), while Ro25-6981 and MPEP did not (Figure 1—figure supplement 5G,H; Ro25-6981 p = 0.670, MPEP p = 0.263).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5D,E with statistical analysis.

claim: Ro25-6981 and MPEP did not reduce PPR disparity in two independent pathway analysis.
source: Consistent with our analysis thus far, bath application of MK801 and AP5 reduced PPR disparity (Figure 1—figure supplement 5D,E; MK801 p = 0.001, AP5 p = 0.004), while Ro25-6981 and MPEP did not (Figure 1—figure supplement 5G,H; Ro25-6981 p = 0.670, MPEP p = 0.263).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5G,H with statistical analysis.

claim: AAV carrying mCherry-tagged nlsCre or a control nls-mCherry was injected bilaterally into the dorsal hippocampus of adult Grin1 floxed mice to knock down astrocyte GluN1.
source: AAV carrying either mCherry-tagged nlsCre (Cre) or a control nls-mCherry lacking Cre or in some experiments control EGFP lacking Cre (Control), all of which were expressed under the GFAP104 promoter, was injected bilaterally into the dorsal hippocampus of adult Grin1 floxed mice (Figure 2A; see Materials and Methods section and E-phys statistics report for details)(Letellier et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology used, with reference to Figure 2A and citation to prior work.

claim: Low titer AAVs (~0.4–4⨯10^10 genome copies/injection) were used to avoid potential reactive astrocytosis.
source: We used low titer AAVs (~0.4–4⨯1010 genome copies/injection) to avoid potential reactive astrocytosis, and although the extent was modest, we obtained a highly specific mCherry expression in astrocytes throughout the area CA1 with little expression in neurons (Figure 2B: Cre, 41.1% ± 2.4% of GFAP+ ve cells [n = 3,529], 0.3% ± 0.1% of NeuN+ ve cells [n = 1,150] from 5 mice; Control, 40.7% ± 1.9% of GFAP+ ve cells [n = 3,309], 0.5% ± 0.1% of NeuN+ ve cells [n = 1,217] from 5 mice).
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology and quantification of viral transduction shown in Figure 2B.

claim: mCherry expression was highly specific to astrocytes throughout the area CA1 with little expression in neurons (Cre: 41.1% ± 2.4% of GFAP+ cells, 0.3% ± 0.1% of NeuN+ cells; Control: 40.7% ± 1.9% of GFAP+ cells, 0.5% ± 0.1% of NeuN+ cells).
source: We used low titer AAVs (~0.4–4⨯1010 genome copies/injection) to avoid potential reactive astrocytosis, and although the extent was modest, we obtained a highly specific mCherry expression in astrocytes throughout the area CA1 with little expression in neurons (Figure 2B: Cre, 41.1% ± 2.4% of GFAP+ ve cells [n = 3,529], 0.3% ± 0.1% of NeuN+ ve cells [n = 1,150] from 5 mice; Control, 40.7% ± 1.9% of GFAP+ ve cells [n = 3,309], 0.5% ± 0.1% of NeuN+ ve cells [n = 1,217] from 5 mice).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Astrocytes that expressed Cre in stratum radiatum showed depolarizing responses to NMDA-glycine puff that were significantly decreased compared to controls.
source: Astrocytes that expressed Cre as identified by the mCherry fluorescence in stratum radiatum (SR) where Schaffer collateral synapses were present, showed depolarizing responses to NMDA-glycine puff that were significantly decreased compared to controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A; P = 0.006).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A with statistical analysis.

claim: mCherry-labeled astrocytes in SO or SLM showed depolarizing responses to NMDA-glycine puff that were not different between Cre and Control slices.
source: In contrast to mCherry-positive astrocytes in SR, mCherry-labeled astrocytes in SO or SLM showed depolarizing responses to NMDA-glycine puff that were not different between Cre and Control slices (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, C; SO p = 0.247; SLM p = 0.268), despite the fact that viral transduction efficiencies were comparable amongst astrocytes across the three layers (SR: Cre 39.8% ± 2.4%, Control 40.2% ± 2.0%; SO: Cre 44.8% ± 3.0%, Control 39.3% ± 5.9%; SLM: Cre 39.1% ± 4.9%, Control 40.0% ± 4.0%).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C with statistical analysis.

claim: The input resistance of patched astrocytes was not altered by Cre expression in any layer.
source: The input resistance of patched astrocytes was not altered by Cre expression in any layer (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: NMDA-glycine responses in SLM were substantially smaller than those in SR or SO.
source: Notably, NMDA-glycine responses in SLM were substantially smaller than those in SR or SO (P = 0.001, one way ANOVA, Bonferroni post-hoc tests).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: AP5 bath application blocked NMDA-glycine puff-induced depolarizing responses in astrocytes in all three layers.
source: Nevertheless, AP5 bath application blocked NMDA-glycine puff-induced depolarizing responses in astrocytes in all three layers.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations described in the text.

claim: Analysis of the relative PPR from two independent Schaffer collateral inputs revealed lower PPR disparity in Cre injected slices compared to control slices.
source: Analysis of the relative PPR from two independent Schaffer collateral inputs also revealed lower PPR disparity in Cre injected slices compared to control slices (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A; p = 0.009).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A with statistical analysis.

claim: The amplitude and frequency of spontaneous EPSCs and the waveform of evoked EPSCs were unaltered by astrocyte-specific GluN1 knock-down.
source: The amplitude and frequency of spontaneous EPSCs and the waveform of evoked EPSCs were unaltered by astrocyte-specific GluN1 knock-down (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B,C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B,C.

claim: In Control slices, AP5 decreased the population variance of PPRs by strengthening some synapses and weakening others.
source: Similar to naive slices, in Control slices, AP5 decreased the population variance of PPRs by strengthening some synapses and weakening others (Figure 2E; Control + AP5 p = 0.017).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E with statistical analysis.

claim: AP5 caused a variable increase in EPSC amplitudes in Control slices.
source: In addition, AP5 caused also a variable increase in EPSC amplitudes (Figure 2G; AP5 p = 0.005) that occurred without a concomitant change in the amplitude or the frequency of spontaneous EPSCs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D,E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 2D,E with statistical analysis.

claim: In Cre slices, the decrease in PPR variance by AP5 was strongly attenuated.
source: In Cre slices, however, the decrease in PPR variance by AP5 was strongly attenuated, despite the modest extent of virus infection in Cre slices (Figure 2F; Cre + AP5 p = 0.789).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F with statistical analysis.

claim: The analysis of PPR disparity across two inputs showed substantially decreased inhibitory effect of AP5 in Cre slices relative to controls.
source: The analysis of PPR disparity across two inputs also showed substantially decreased inhibitory effect of AP5 in Cre slices relative to controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 2H,I; Control + AP5 p = 0.013, Cre + AP5 p = 0.315).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2H,I with statistical analysis.

claim: The small increase in EPSC amplitudes observed upon applying AP5 was attenuated in Cre slices.
source: Curiously, the small increase in EPSC amplitudes observed upon applying AP5 was also attenuated in Cre slices (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Release probability variations were modelled based on gamma distributions.
source: We first modelled release probability variations based on gamma distributions (Buzsáki and Mizuseki, 2014; Branco and Staras, 2009; Murthy et al., 1997).
evidence: This describes the modeling approach with citations to prior literature.

claim: Release probability was estimated using the styryl dye FM1-43 in synaptic networks of hippocampal pyramidal neurons co-cultured with astrocytes.
source: To achieve this, we experimentally obtained estimates of release probability using the styryl dye, FM1-43 in synaptic networks of hippocampal pyramidal neurons co-cultured with astrocytes.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology used to obtain data for modeling.

claim: Neurons were extracellularly stimulated with 40 action potentials at 20 Hz in the presence of FM1-43 to label the readily releasable vesicle pool, a parameter related to release probability.
source: Briefly, neurons were extracellularly stimulated with 40 action potentials at 20 Hz in the presence of FM1-43 to label the readily releasable vesicle pool, a parameter related to release probability (Rosenmund and Stevens, 1996; Letellier et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology with citations to prior literature.

claim: The gamma distribution for the AP5 condition showed a smaller variance than that of the control condition.
source: Notably, the gamma distribution for the AP5 condition showed a smaller variance than that of the control condition, which was reminiscent of the effect of bath applied AP5 on PPR distribution.
evidence: This is an observation from the modeling analysis based on FM1-43 data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Simulations using the decreased release probability variance of the AP5 condition showed little change in LTD whereas LTP was compromised compared to the control condition.
source: Simulations using the decreased release probability variance of the AP5 condition showed little change in LTD whereas LTP was compromised compared to the control condition.
evidence: This is a result from the computational modeling shown in Figure 3B.

claim: A less variable release probability represented by the AP5 condition required higher levels of current injection to trigger LTP compared to a broad release probability distribution represented by the control condition.
source: Specifically, when the efficacy of synaptic weight change was compared as a function of the amplitude of the postsynaptic current injection A2, a less variable release probability represented by the AP5 condition required higher levels of current injection to trigger LTP compared to a broad release probability distribution represented by the control condition (Figure 3B, left versus middle panel).
evidence: This is a result from the computational modeling shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The effect of narrowed release probability variance in increasing the threshold for eliciting LTP persisted also for the AP5-with-control mean group.
source: The effect of narrowed release probability variance in increasing the threshold for eliciting LTP persisted also for the AP5-with-control mean group (Figure 3B, right panel).
evidence: This is a result from the computational modeling shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The control condition exhibited a higher propensity to undergo LTP compared to the two AP5 groups representing conditions of reduced release probability variance.
source: The analysis clearly revealed that the potentiation was more sensitive for smaller input current impulses. In effect, the results showed that the control condition exhibited a higher propensity to undergo LTP compared to the two AP5 groups representing conditions of reduced release probability variance.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the computational modeling analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Spike inputs that promote potentiation under control condition tend to favor weaker potentiation in either AP5 or AP5-with-control mean conditions.
source: The plots indicate that spike inputs that promote potentiation under control condition tend to favor weaker potentiation in either AP5 or AP5-with-control mean, and spike inputs that promote depression under control condition tend to favor weaker depression in either AP5 or AP5-with-control mean.
evidence: This is a result from the computational modeling shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Spike inputs that promote depression under control condition tend to favor weaker depression in either AP5 or AP5-with-control mean conditions.
source: The plots indicate that spike inputs that promote potentiation under control condition tend to favor weaker potentiation in either AP5 or AP5-with-control mean, and spike inputs that promote depression under control condition tend to favor weaker depression in either AP5 or AP5-with-control mean.
evidence: This is a result from the computational modeling shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Reducing the variance of the release probability distribution without a change in the mean had a stronger effect in compromising LTP than LTD.
source: When the absolute average difference in the extent of LTP or LTD relative to control was compared between the two AP5 conditions, reducing the variance of the release probability distribution without a change in the mean had a stronger effect in compromising LTP than LTD, while in the AP5 condition, both potentiation and depression were similarly affected (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a result from the computational modeling shown in Figure 4C.

claim: All putative astrocytes had low input resistances (SR 11.20 ± 0.36 MΩ; SO 13.24 ± 0.43 MΩ; SLM 10.60 ± 0.33 MΩ), lacked action potentials, and displayed linear current-voltage relationships.
source: All putative astrocytes had low input resistances (SR 11.20 ± 0.36 MΩ; SO 13.24 ± 0.43 MΩ; SLM 10.60 ± 0.33 MΩ; n = 39 cells from 9 mice sampled for each layer), lacked action potentials, and displayed linear current-voltage relationships (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: CA1 pyramidal neurons expressed high levels of Grin1, Grin2a, and Grin2b subunit mRNAs but expressed substantially low levels of Grin2c mRNA.
source: CA1 pyramidal neurons expressed high levels of Grin1, Grin2a, and Grin2b subunit mRNAs but expressed substantially low levels of Grin2c mRNA.
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Astrocytes in all three layers showed robust expression of Grin2c mRNA.
source: In contrast, astrocytes in all three layers showed robust expression of Grin2c mRNA.
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Astrocytes showed minimal expression of Grin2a and Grin2b mRNAs.
source: Moreover, astrocytes showed minimal expression of Grin2a and Grin2b mRNAs, and the Grin1 mRNA expression in astrocytes was also substantially low compared to neurons (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Grin1 mRNA expression in astrocytes was substantially low compared to neurons.
source: Moreover, astrocytes showed minimal expression of Grin2a and Grin2b mRNAs, and the Grin1 mRNA expression in astrocytes was also substantially low compared to neurons (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Grin2d mRNA in CA1 pyramidal neurons and astrocytes was undetectable in RNA extracted from patch clamping both cell types while the probe itself could detect Grin2d mRNA in brain tissue extracts.
source: Grin2d mRNA in CA1 pyramidal neurons and astrocytes was also tested, and it was undetectable in RNA extracted from patch clamping both cell types while the probe itself could detect Grin2d mRNA in brain tissue extracts (data not shown).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from RT-PCR analysis.

claim: The expression of GluN2C subunit protein in the hippocampus was confirmed by immunoprecipitation of mouse hippocampal extracts followed by Western blotting.
source: The expression of GluN2C subunit protein in the hippocampus was confirmed by immunoprecipitation of mouse hippocampal extracts followed by Western blotting, using an antibody against the Cre recombinase that is not expressed in wild type mice, as a negative control (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by biochemical data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The hippocampus of Grin2ciCre/+ mice crossed with Ai9 reporter line showed robust tdTomato fluorescence in astrocytes identified by GFAP labelling (81.6% ± 5.7% of GFAP+ cells).
source: The hippocampus of the offspring showed robust tdTomato fluorescence in astrocytes identified by GFAP labelling (81.6% ± 5.7% of GFAP+ ve cells; Figure 5E and F), which was consistent with the high expression level of GluN2C mRNA in astrocytes (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5E,F.

claim: Some interneurons in SR identified by NeuN labeling expressed tdTomato (3.6% ± 1.6% of NeuN+ cells in SR) in Grin2ciCre/+ x Ai9 mice.
source: Moreover, some interneurons in SR identified by the NeuN labeling also expressed tdTomato (3.6% ± 1.6% of NeuN+ ve cells in SR, Figure 5E and F), which was in agreement with previous reports (Ravikrishnan et al., 2018; Gupta et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5E,F and citations to prior literature.

claim: The pyramidal cell layer showed sporadic tdTomato-labeled neuronal cell bodies (5.8% ± 1.0% of NeuN+ cells in stratum pyramidale) in Grin2ciCre/+ x Ai9 mice.
source: Surprisingly, the pyramidal cell layer also showed sporadic tdTomato-labeled neuronal cell bodies, although such cells represented a limited proportion of pyramidal neurons (5.8% ± 1.0% of NeuN+ ve cells in stratum pyramidale, Figure 5E and F).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5E,F.

claim: A linear fit to the ΔPPR vs baseline PPR data for QNZ46 intercepted the x-axis near the baseline mean PPR (X intercept = 2.07).
source: Again we observed the negative correlation between the change in PPR and the baseline PPR (Figure 6A, bottom), with a linear fit to the data intercepting the x-axis near the baseline mean PPR (X intercept = 2.07).
evidence: This is an analysis of the data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Bath application of QNZ46 decreased the PPR disparity in two independent pathway analysis.
source: Additionally, in experiments monitoring two independent Schaffer collateral inputs, bath application of QNZ46 decreased the PPR disparity as found for AP5 and MK801 (Figure 1—figure supplement 5F; p = 0.005).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5F with statistical analysis.

claim: QNZ46 bath application caused a significant increase in EPSC amplitudes.
source: When EPSC amplitudes were examined, QNZ46 bath application caused a significant increase, reminiscent of the changes observed upon AP5 and MK801 application (Figure 6D; p = 0.014).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D with statistical analysis.

claim: QNZ46 significantly increased CV–2 of EPSC amplitudes.
source: Moreover, similarly to AP5, QNZ46 significantly increased CV–2 of EPSC amplitudes (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B; p = 0.009), which was suggestive of presynaptic alterations.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B with statistical analysis.

claim: In control slices, QNZ46 decreased the PPR variance.
source: In control slices QNZ46 decreased the PPR variance (Figure 6B; p = 0.065) and caused a variable increase in EPSC amplitudes (Figure 6E; p = 0.005) without a concomitant change in the amplitude or the frequency of spontaneous EPSCs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B with statistical analysis.

claim: QNZ46 was no longer effective in producing a significant change in the PPR variance in Cre slices.
source: Crucially, as observed for AP5, QNZ46 was no longer effective in producing a significant change in the PPR variance in Cre slices (Figure 6C; p = 0.649).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C with statistical analysis.

claim: QNZ46 decreased the PPR disparity in a manner that was sensitive to astrocyte GluN1 knock-down.
source: When PPR disparity across two inputs was monitored, QNZ46 decreased the PPR disparity in a manner that was sensitive to astrocyte GluN1 knock-down, which also supported the involvement for GluN2C-NMDARs in regulating presynaptic strength diversity (Figure 2—figure supplement 2J,K; Control + QNZ46 p = 0.031; Cre + QNZ46 p = 0.126).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2J,K with statistical analysis.

claim: QNZ46-dependent increase of EPSC amplitudes was attenuated in Cre slices.
source: Moreover, similarly to AP5, QNZ46-dependent increase of EPSC amplitudes was attenuated also in Cre slices (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: GluN2C mRNA is expressed relatively evenly across SR, SO, and SLM layers in CA1 astrocytes compared to CA1 pyramidal neurons.
source: Our RT-PCR analysis of NMDAR subtype expression showed relatively high expression of GluN2C mRNA across SR, SO, and SLM layers in CA1 astrocytes compared to CA1 pyramidal neurons.
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: SR astrocytes showed the highest sensitivity to astrocyte GluN1 knock-down in NMDA-glycine puff application responses.
source: Nevertheless, despite the relatively even expression of GluN2C across layers, our experiments monitoring NMDA-glycine puff application responses in CA1 astrocytes revealed layer-specific differences in the GluN1-dependent component of the slow depolarizing responses triggered by the NMDA-glycine puff, with SR astrocytes showing the highest sensitivity to the astrocyte GluN1 knock-down (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Neither MK801 nor AP5 had any appreciable effect on PPR variance in SO.
source: Neither MK801 nor AP5 had any appreciable effect on PPR variance in SO (Figure 7E and G: MK801, p = 0.107; AP5 p = 0.472) and SLM (Figure 7I and K: MK801, p = 0.920; AP5, p = 0.741).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E,G with statistical analysis.

claim: Neither MK801 nor AP5 had any appreciable effect on PPR variance in SLM.
source: Neither MK801 nor AP5 had any appreciable effect on PPR variance in SO (Figure 7E and G: MK801, p = 0.107; AP5 p = 0.472) and SLM (Figure 7I and K: MK801, p = 0.920; AP5, p = 0.741).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7I,K with statistical analysis.

claim: MK801 modestly increased EPSC amplitudes at some inputs in SO but had no effect in SLM.
source: MK801 modestly increased EPSC amplitudes at some inputs in SO (Figure 7F: p = 0.783) but it had no effect in SLM (Figure 7J: p = 0.915).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7F,J with statistical analysis.

claim: AP5 significantly depressed EPSC amplitudes in SO.
source: Moreover, AP5 did not potentiate EPSC amplitudes as observed for the SR input, but instead it significantly depressed EPSC amplitudes in SO (Figure 7H: p = 0.028) while it caused no appreciable change in SLM (Figure 7L: p = 0.317).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7H with statistical analysis.

claim: AP5 caused no appreciable change in EPSC amplitudes in SLM.
source: Moreover, AP5 did not potentiate EPSC amplitudes as observed for the SR input, but instead it significantly depressed EPSC amplitudes in SO (Figure 7H: p = 0.028) while it caused no appreciable change in SLM (Figure 7L: p = 0.317).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7L with statistical analysis.

claim: Neither MK801 nor AP5 depressed the PPR disparity of the SO and the SLM inputs in two independent pathway analysis.
source: As a further test of the layer specificity of astrocyte NMDAR-dependent regulation of PPR variability, we assessed PPR disparity by performing two independent pathway analysis in each layer in response to bath applied NMDAR antagonists. Again, in contrast to SR input (Figure 1—figure supplement 5D, E), neither MK801 nor AP5 depressed the PPR disparity of the SO and the SLM inputs (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Astrocyte NMDARs, and particularly GluN2C NMDARs, maintain the diversity of PPR specifically of SR inputs to CA1 pyramidal neurons.
source: These observations are consistent with the role for astrocyte NMDARs, and particularly GluN2C NMDARs, for maintaining the diversity of PPR specifically of SR inputs to CA1 pyramidal neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in Figures 1, 2, 6, and 7.

claim: Broad heterogeneity in the efficacy of synaptic transmission is a fundamental feature of small glutamatergic synapses in the mammalian brain.
source: Broad heterogeneity in the efficacy of synaptic transmission is a fundamental feature of small glutamatergic synapses in the mammalian brain (Dobrunz and Stevens, 1997; Atwood and Karunanithi, 2002; Branco and Staras, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: A variety of presynaptic parameters contribute to the observed variability in synaptic transmission efficacy, such as the abundance, subtype, and location of presynaptic calcium channels, their positioning with respect to the synaptic vesicles, the active zone size and the number of docked vesicles, the state of vesicle fusion machinery, as well as the coupling to neuromodulatory signals, and the synapse's recent history of synaptic plasticity.
source: A variety of presynaptic parameters contribute to the observed variability, such as the abundance, subtype, and location of presynaptic calcium channels (Thalhammer et al., 2017; Brenowitz and Regehr, 2007; Éltes et al., 2017), their positioning with respect to the synaptic vesicles, the active zone size and the number of docked vesicles, the state of vesicle fusion machinery (Park et al., 2012; Marra et al., 2012; Fulterer et al., 2018; Glebov et al., 2017; Holderith et al., 2012), as well as the coupling to neuromodulatory signals (Burke et al., 2018), and the synapse's recent history of synaptic plasticity.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Astrocyte GluN2C NMDAR signaling broadens the range of basal release efficacy of Schaffer collateral synapses by effectively maintaining strong synapses stronger and weaker synapses weaker without an overt effect on the mean synaptic strength.
source: Our study highlights the novel contribution of astrocyte GluN2C NMDAR signaling in broadening the range of basal release efficacy of Schaffer collateral synapses by effectively maintaining strong synapses stronger and weaker synapses weaker without an overt effect on the mean synaptic strength.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: PPR is inversely related to presynaptic release probability.
source: The present study took advantage of paired-pulse response as a measure of presynaptic efficacy. While PPR – a form of short-term plasticity – is inversely related to presynaptic release probability (Dobrunz and Stevens, 1997), it does not necessarily always represent changes in presynaptic release across all conditions.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: PPR changes can arise from a postsynaptic mechanism involving changes in the extent accumulation of desensitized AMPA receptors at the postsynaptic density.
source: For example, PPR changes can arise from a postsynaptic mechanism involving changes in the extent accumulation of desensitized AMPA receptors at the postsynaptic density (Heine et al., 2008; Frischknecht et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Sampling a small number of synapses by a relatively weak stimulation intensity consistently revealed a component of PPR distribution that was regulated by astrocyte NMDARs.
source: Sampling a small number of synapses by a relatively weak stimulation intensity (i.e. mean EPSC amplitude of ~60 ± 6 pA to Schaffer collateral stimulation in control condition) consistently revealed a component of PPR distribution that was regulated by astrocyte NMDARs.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: Such modulation by astrocyte NMDARs could be masked when sampling a large synapse population that yields stable ensemble responses.
source: Notably, such modulation could be masked when sampling a large synapse population that yields stable ensemble responses (Lines et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Several studies have implicated astrocyte signaling in LTD in hippocampal CA3 to CA1 synapses.
source: Notably, several studies have implicated astrocyte signaling in LTD in hippocampal CA3 to CA1 synapses (Chen et al., 2013; Andrade-Talavera et al., 2016; Navarrete et al., 2019; Pinto-Duarte et al., 2019), where spike timing-dependent LTD in slices from young mice is sensitive to inhibitors of GluN2C/D, although the source of GluN2C/D remains to be determined (Andrade-Talavera et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Astrocyte GluN2C NMDAR-dependent maintenance of variable basal presynaptic strengths of CA3 to CA1 synapses could be linked to astrocyte signaling that promotes LTP and LTD.
source: Astrocyte GluN2C NMDAR-dependent maintenance of variable basal presynaptic strengths of CA3 to CA1 synapses that we have identified here could therefore be linked to astrocyte signaling that promotes LTP and LTD, which in turn, are not only important for learning and memory but also for network stability (Collingridge et al., 2010; Royer and Paré, 2003; Zenke and Gerstner, 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative statement linking the findings to broader implications, supported by citations.

claim: The GluN2C NMDAR-dependent broadening of the basal presynaptic efficacy in CA1 neurons is confined to the SR inputs and not observed for SO or SLM inputs.
source: Curiously, this GluN2C NMDAR-dependent broadening of the basal presynaptic efficacy in CA1 neurons is confined to the SR inputs and not observed for SO or SLM inputs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in Figure 7.

claim: For dendritic computations in CA1 pyramidal neurons, the broad variability of synaptic strengths at CA3-CA1 synapses is more crucial compared to the synaptic strength variability of basal or apical tuft inputs.
source: This suggests that for dendritic computations in CA1 pyramidal neurons, the broad variability of synaptic strengths at CA3-CA1 synapses is more crucial compared to the synaptic strength variability of basal or apical tuft inputs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the layer-specific findings.

claim: Mice deficient in GluN2C show deficits in acquisition of conditioned fear and working memory and changes in neuronal oscillations.
source: Mice deficient in GluN2C, while mostly normal in their behavior, show deficits in acquisition of conditioned fear and working memory and changes in neuronal oscillations (Hillman et al., 2011; Mao et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Some population of interneurons express GluN2C.
source: Some population of interneurons express GluN2C, however (Gupta et al., 2016; Ravikrishnan et al., 2018), and this confounds the interpretation of the observed effects solely to deficits in astrocyte GluN2C.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The narrowing of the range of PPR upon astrocyte NMDAR inhibition suggests a capacity for astrocytes to impose dual modulatory actions downstream of astrocyte GluN2C NMDARs.
source: The narrowing of the range of PPR upon astrocyte NMDAR inhibition suggests a capacity for astrocytes to impose dual modulatory actions downstream of astrocyte GluN2C NMDARs, in one possibility, involving the release of two types of gliotransmitters with one potentiating and another depressing synaptic transmission (Schwarz et al., 2017; Covelo and Araque, 2018).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings, supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Astrocyte-mediated release of ATP, which is converted to adenosine by extracellular ATPases, has been implicated in the bi-directional modulation of presynaptic efficacy.
source: In some cases, the release of a single molecule may also suffice: astrocyte-mediated release of ATP, which is converted to adenosine by extracellular ATPases, has been implicated in the bi-directional modulation of presynaptic efficacy (Panatier et al., 2011; Pascual et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2003; Tan et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The effects of adenosine depend in part on the presynaptic A2A or A1 receptors that either enhance or suppress presynaptic function, respectively.
source: The effects of adenosine depend in part on the presynaptic A2A or A1 receptors that either enhance or suppress presynaptic function, respectively (Panatier et al., 2011; Tan et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: At the neuromuscular junction, a stronger synaptic input is preferentially potentiated further by the activation of presynaptic A2A receptors while the weaker one remains unchanged or slightly depressed.
source: At the neuromuscular junction, where glial cells mediate synaptic competition involving glial purinergic signaling, it has been shown that a stronger synaptic input is preferentially potentiated further by the activation of presynaptic A2A receptors while the weaker one remains unchanged or slightly depressed (Darabid et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Previous transcriptome analysis of the major cell types in mouse cerebral cortex suggested that the GluN2C NMDAR subunit mRNA is one of the highly enriched transcripts in astrocytes, whose level can be up to 70-fold of the level found in neurons.
source: Previous transcriptome analysis of the major cell types in mouse cerebral cortex have suggested that the GluN2C NMDAR subunit mRNA is one of the highly enriched transcripts in astrocytes, whose level can be up to 70-fold of the level found in neurons (Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The discordance between the detected GluN1 and GluN2C mRNA levels in astrocytes could be explained if the mRNAs are differentially localized, with GluN1 mRNA being preferentially targeted to processes compared to the cell body of astrocytes.
source: The whole-cell patch clamp method we used to collect RNAs is biased towards sampling of transcripts that are abundant in the cell body. Given that astrocyte processes are numerous and thin, the discordance between the detected GluN1 and GluN2C mRNA levels could be explained if the mRNAs are differentially localized, with GluN1 mRNA being preferentially targeted to processes compared to the cell body of astrocytes.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed data.

claim: A recent study reported GluN1 mRNA in astrocyte processes that is locally translated.
source: Such a proposal is consistent with a recent study reporting of GluN1 mRNA in astrocyte processes that is locally translated (Sakers et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The layer-specificity of synaptic modulation by astrocyte GluN2C NMDARs could potentially arise from features of GluN2C NMDAR assembly and trafficking and/or signaling that is unique to SR astrocytes over SO and SLM astrocytes.
source: Therefore, the layer-specificity of synaptic modulation could potentially arise from features of GluN2C NMDAR assembly and trafficking and/or signaling that is unique to SR astrocytes over SO and SLM astrocytes.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed layer-specific effects.

claim: Differences in the properties of presynaptic inputs to CA1 pyramidal neuron dendrites across layers could contribute to layer-specific synaptic modulation by astrocyte GluN2C NMDARs.
source: Additionally, differences in the properties of presynaptic inputs to CA1 pyramidal neuron dendrites across layers (e.g. Schroeder et al., 2018) could also contribute to layer-specific synaptic modulation by astrocyte GluN2C NMDARs.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The GluN2C subunit forms diheteromeric receptor complexes with the obligate GluN1 subunit and triheteromeric receptor complexes with GluN1 and GluN2A.
source: The GluN2C subunit forms diheteromeric receptor complexes with the obligate GluN1 subunit and triheteromeric receptor complexes with GluN1 and GluN2A (Paoletti et al., 2013; Hansen et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: GluN2C-containing NMDARs show reduced channel open probability, increased glutamate sensitivity, slow receptor deactivation, and a decreased sensitivity to Mg2+ block.
source: For example, GluN2C-containing NMDARs show reduced channel open probability, increased glutamate sensitivity, slow receptor deactivation, and a decreased sensitivity to Mg2+ block (Paoletti et al., 2013; Hansen et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Weak Mg2+ binding of GluN2C-containing NMDARs would enable open-pore blockers such as MK801 to rapidly exert their inhibitory action.
source: Weak Mg2+ binding would enable open-pore blockers such as MK801, to nonetheless rapidly exert their inhibitory action.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known properties of GluN2C-containing NMDARs.

claim: The reduced Mg2+ sensitivity of astrocyte GluN2C NMDARs could have contributed to the rapid effect observed for MK801 in normalizing presynaptic strengths and reducing the PPR disparity.
source: Such reduced Mg2+ sensitivity of astrocyte GluN2C NMDARs could have contributed to the rapid effect observed for MK801 in normalizing presynaptic strengths and reducing the PPR disparity.
evidence: This is an inference linking the properties of GluN2C-containing NMDARs to the experimental observations.

claim: The low EC50 of GluN2C-containing NMDAR activation to glutamate suggests that they may be well suited for detecting synaptic release events at perisynaptic astrocyte processes that can be at some distance from the active zone.
source: Moreover, the low EC50 of GluN2C-containing NMDAR activation to glutamate (Hansen et al., 2018) suggests that they may be well suited for detecting synaptic release events at perisynaptic astrocyte processes that can be at some distance from the active zone.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known properties of GluN2C-containing NMDARs, supported by a citation.

claim: Under physiological conditions, GluN2C/GluN2D-containing NMDARs display up to 10-fold higher sensitivity to ketamine and memantine in comparison to GluN2A/GluN2B-containing NMDARs.
source: Under physiological conditions, GluN2C/GluN2D-containing NMDARs display up to 10-fold higher sensitivity to ketamine and memantine in comparison to GluN2A/GluN2B-containing NMDARs that are highly expressed in neurons (Kotermanski and Johnson, 2009; Hansen et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: It would be crucial to consider the consequences of interfering with GluN2C NMDARs that are enriched in astrocytes when developing therapeutics targeting NMDARs.
source: Therefore, although therapeutics targeting NMDARs to date have largely focused on neuronal NMDARs, it would be crucial to consider also the consequences of interfering with GluN2C NMDARs that are enriched in astrocytes, which is underscored by the increasing recognition of the involvement of astrocytes in a variety of neurological disorders (Zuchero and Barres, 2015; Chung et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the findings, supported by citations to prior literature.
